meta.title: Operation of Digital Kymograph in Pharmacology Laboratory

sections.purpose: To digitally record and display physiological signals including isotonic and isometric contractions of isolated tissues, nerve-muscle preparations, and cardiovascular responses during pharmacology experiments.
sections.scope: Applicable to Pharmacology laboratory for recording smooth muscle contractions, cardiac preparations, nerve-muscle experiments, and drug dose-response data in isolated organ experiments.
procedure: Connect the digital kymograph to the power supply and to the data acquisition system or PC via USB/RS-232 interface.
Install and open the appropriate recording software (LabChart, PowerLab, or equivalent).
Connect the transducer output cable from the force transducer or isotonic lever to the appropriate input channel of the digital kymograph.
Calibrate the system: apply a known force (e.g., 1 g, 2 g weights) to the transducer and note the corresponding digital readout to establish the calibration factor.
Set the recording parameters in software: sampling rate (typically 100–1000 Hz for muscle contractions), time axis scale, and amplitude scale.
Zero the baseline: with no load applied, set the baseline to zero on the recording channel.
Set up the organ bath or muscle preparation as per the experimental protocol.
Start the recording session in the software before administering drugs.
Apply test doses of drugs and observe the digitally recorded contraction or relaxation responses.
Mark each drug addition event using the event marker channel in the software.
After the experiment, stop the recording and save the data file.
Analyze the recorded traces: measure amplitude, duration, latency, and calculate dose-response parameters.
Export data for statistical analysis or prepare printed kymograph traces for the laboratory record.
Disconnect the transducer gently; clean and store as per protocol.
Log the experiment details, drug doses, and observations in the laboratory notebook.
precautions: Handle transducer connections with care — excessive force on the transducer cable connector damages the input socket.
Do not exceed the maximum input voltage/force rating of the transducer — overloading damages the sensor element.
Ensure the grounding of all electronic equipment is proper — ground loops cause 50 Hz electrical noise in recordings.
Calibrate at the beginning of every experimental session — transducer sensitivity can drift.
Save data files frequently — an unexpected software or power failure will lose unsaved recordings.
Keep the electronic unit away from water and Tyrode's solution — moisture causes irreversible damage.
Back up all experimental data files to a secondary location (USB/network drive) at the end of each session.
